title: Four passages
intro:
*Five minutes. Commit before you look.*

Four passages from the **factual findings** section of investigation reports: the section that should contain observations and corroboration, and nothing above rung two.

**One of them keeps every sentence on the rung its section is supposed to occupy.** Find it. Then look at what the other three did, because two of them are wrong in ways that read as careful writing.

artifacts.label: Passage 1
artifacts.body: "On 14 March the respondent became visibly frustrated during the team meeting and was dismissive of the complainant's concerns about the project timeline. Two witnesses confirmed the atmosphere was tense. The respondent's manner throughout appears to have been intended to shut down further discussion, although he denies this was his purpose. The complainant found the exchange humiliating."

artifacts.label: Passage 2
artifacts.body: "The complainant states that on 14 March the respondent 'shouted' at her during a team meeting. The respondent states that 'voices were raised on both sides'. Witness A recalls raised voices and attributes them to both parties. Witness B describes 'nothing I'd call unusual'. Witness C was present per the meeting invitation but was not interviewed, as she left the organisation before the investigation commenced; no statement was obtained. The meeting invitation records the date as 14 March. No contemporaneous notes of the meeting exist."

artifacts.label: Passage 3
artifacts.body: "The complainant alleges that on 14 March the respondent shouted at her. This is denied. Having considered the accounts of the complainant, the respondent and two witnesses, and noting that the respondent's account is internally consistent while the complainant's account of the sequence of events shifted between her written complaint and her interview, I find on the balance of probabilities that voices were raised by both parties and that the respondent did not shout."

artifacts.label: Passage 4
artifacts.body: "On 14 March there was an incident in a team meeting involving the complainant and the respondent. Accounts of what occurred vary. The complainant's account is set out at Appendix 2 and the respondent's at Appendix 3. Witness statements are at Appendix 4. The evidence is finely balanced and it is not possible to be certain what was said. It should be noted that the complainant has raised concerns about this respondent previously, in 2023, although that matter was not substantiated."

reasoning:
**Passage 2 stays on rung two throughout, and the tell is that every sentence is attributed or sourced.** Quotes in the complainant's and respondent's own words. Each witness's account attributed to that witness. The document record cited separately. And two things most passages omit entirely: **the witness who was not interviewed, with the reason**, and **the absence of contemporaneous notes.** That is Lesson 1's fourth element (*what could not be established, and why*) appearing where it belongs rather than being quietly skipped.

Notice it makes no finding, and that is correct for a factual-findings section. The finding goes in the findings section, allegation by allegation, and a reader can see exactly which evidence it was built from.

**Passage 1 is the module's central failure, and it reads like competent writing.** Four rung breaches in five sentences. *"Became visibly frustrated"* and *"was dismissive"*: evaluative adjectives doing the work of findings, and no witness said either word. *"Two witnesses confirmed the atmosphere was tense"* — "confirmed" asserts that a contested thing is established, and "tense" is a characterization attributed to witnesses who probably described conduct. *"Appears to have been intended to shut down further discussion"*: a **state-of-mind determination**, hedged with *appears* in a way that provides no protection at all. And *"found the exchange humiliating"* is the complainant's account presented as fact rather than as her account. At a hearing you will be asked to justify each of these as a conclusion, and you may not remember reaching them.

**Passage 3 is well-written and in the wrong section**, which makes it the useful distractor. As a *findings* paragraph it is close to exemplary: the standard is named, the reasoning is visible, the credibility assessment is explicit and attributed to the author. In the **factual findings** section it is a rung-four determination sitting where rung-two material belongs — and worse, it means the credibility assessment (*"the complainant's account of the sequence shifted"*) has been made before the evidence has been set out, so no reader can check the reasoning against the record. Right content, wrong place, and the misplacement destroys the auditability the elements structure exists for.

**Passage 4 avoids every rung breach and fails differently.** Nothing is characterized, nothing is concluded, everything is appended. It is also **empty**: *"accounts vary"*, *"the evidence is finely balanced"*, *"it is not possible to be certain"*, a reader learns nothing about what any account actually said, and the appendices are doing work the report should do. Then the last sentence is the serious problem. **The unsubstantiated 2023 matter has no place here.** It is prejudicial, it was not substantiated, it is not the allegation under investigation, and including it invites exactly the inference nobody has stated. Rung-clean and still the passage most likely to be read against you.

The transferable test: **for each sentence, ask who said it.** In Passage 2 every sentence has an answer: a party, a witness, a document, or explicitly nobody. In 1 and 3 several sentences have only one possible author, which is you, and in a factual section that is a rung breach whether or not the conclusion is right.
